ImageDescription.value: This photo captures a vibrant salad bar or buffet display featuring an assortment of fresh ingredients arranged in stainless steel serving containers. The colorful spread includes shredded carrots, cherry tomatoes, diced ham or bell peppers, corn kernels, kidney beans, sliced red onions, shredded cheese, leafy green lettuce, red cabbage, croutons, ice (for keeping items chilled), diced cucumber, olives, and what appears to be green gelatin or a similar dessert item. Each container has its own serving utensil, and the metallic surfaces and dim lighting give the scene a typical restaurant or cafeteria ambiance. The variety of colors - bright oranges, deep reds, greens, yellows, and purples - creates an appetizing and visually appealing presentation of build-your-own salad options.

ImageDescription.value: This image shows maize corns placed on a traditional drying rack locally known as a sak in a rural village of Kullu district, Himachal Pradesh, India. Drying maize in this manner is a common post-harvest practice used to preserve the crop for storage and winter consumption. Maize is one of the staple foods of the region and is traditionally grown alongside rajmah (kidney beans) in mixed cropping systems.

Burpee's Bush Lima The bushes grow eighteen to twenty
inches, of stout growth and always erect,

Pole or Running Beans
Lazy Wife's No good wife would
like to be called "a lazy wife," yet
she will be excused for exhibiting a
lazy spell when bean picking time
comes, if she has the foresight to
plant this variety. They are called
Lazy Wive's because they hang so
full and the pods are so long and
broad that a mess is soon picked.
The pods are green, wonderfully
broad. thick, fleshy and entirely
stringless, retaining all their good
qualitis until nearly ripe. The
peculiar taste and agreeable flavor
of this bean are so captivating that
other varieties are not desired while the
Lazy Wives can be obtained.
Pint 25c; quart 45c.

Improved Golden
Wax
In spite of all the new sorts of beans
being introduced every year, our
trade calls for more Golden Wax
than any other variety. This great
popularity is due largely to the fact
that the variety we have is a great
improvement on the old Golden

ImageDescription.value:
Cast copper alloy double-loop buckle with an openwork frame that is vesica shaped in plan and D-shaped in section with straight inner edges, creating two kidney-bean shaped loops within the frame. The strap bar divides these loops and is narrowed and flush with the frame. Around the inner edge of the frame there is a rouletted recessed border. At oblique angles to the border there are moulded transverse lines, which extend to the outer edge of the frame, and define foliate ovoids between them, making the surface appear like a vine. There are four circular apertures, two at either end of the buckle, within the cusped outer edges, and two at either end of the strap bar, within slight semi-circular protrusions.

Whitehead (1996) illustrates a similar buckle on page 69, No.434, which is dated from c.1550-1660.
